title: Mixed-topic questions: Paper 2
subtitle: The blends the examiners set on Paper 2: two or three topics in one question, and the join between them
lede: The long questions on Paper 2 hand a quantity from one topic to the next — an energy, a force, a volume, a potential difference — and the marks sit at the hand-over. This page collects the blends that the June 2023, 2024 and 2025 Paper 2 questions set: density into latent heat, pressure into forces and particles, springs into force diagrams, upthrust into moments, work into efficiency and power, electricity into energy and heat, and induction into the devices around it. Each section names the join, lays the chain out as a table, works one example modelled on the real question with new numbers, and practises the hand-over. The physics of every stage is on its topic page — this page is about carrying the number across. Sections and parts that are Higher or Physics only carry their tag.
howto: Start with M1 and learn the four habits: find the join, match the units there, carry forward and label, check the number makes sense.
Before each chain, say which quantity each stage hands to the next and what unit it must be in. Then do the arithmetic.
Do every multi-part question in one go on paper, EWAU for each stage, before checking any part — in the exam the parts come together.
For the written parts, write the chain in full sentences with the physics object as the subject, then compare with the model answer line by line.
If a stage is red, go back to its topic page (the section is named in the chain table) before moving on.
Fill in the traffic-light self-check at the end of each section. Anything red or amber is what to revise next.

sections.title: Finding the join: how a blended question hands over from one topic to the next

parts.title: The four habits
parts.html:
HabitWhy it scoresExample
Find the joineach stage of a chain has its own equation; the output of one is the input of the nextGPE from a height → the same number as KE → a speed from $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$
Match units at the jointhe examiners' reports name the same slips every year: kJ left as kJ, cm in a squared term, minutes into $E = Pt$, mm² into $P = F/A$$E = Pt$ needs seconds: 5.0 minutes is 300 s
Carry forward and labelmark schemes give a mark per stage and allow "error carried forward" — a wrong stage 1 still lets the equation and substitution marks of stages 2 and 3 score if they use it and are shown — usually the evaluation mark too (June 2025 1H Q8(a)(ii), 2H Q2(a)(ii)), though not always (1H Q6(a)(ii): "no ecf for evaluation")June 2025 2H Q9(a)(ii): starting from the wrong upthrust still scored 3 of 4
Check the join makes sensea speed of 300 m/s for a trolley, a pool 35 m deep, a spring constant of 2.5 N/m for a stiff spring — the number itself tells you a join went wrong"look at the result of a calculation to see if the value makes sense" (June 2025 report)

The chains on this page are the ones that have come up in the June 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers for this paper. Each section names the join, lays the chain out as a table, and works one example modelled on the real question with new numbers. The physics of each stage is on its topic page — this page practises the hand-over.

parts.title: A trolley, a runway and a staircase
parts.question: A trolley is lifted onto a runway 0.30 m high and gains 4.8 J of gravitational potential energy. (a) Show that the mass of the trolley is about 1.6 kg. (b) Calculate the speed the trolley would have at the bottom of the runway if all the GPE became kinetic energy. (c) The measured speed is 2.1 m/s. Suggest why. (d) A student of mass 52 kg runs up a 3.0 m staircase in 4.0 s; calculate her power. ($g = 10$ N/kg; 9 marks)
steps: (a) Stage 1, Topic 3: $\Delta GPE = m g \Delta h$, so $m = \Delta GPE \div (g \Delta h) = 4.8 \div (10 \times 0.30) = 1.6$ kg.
(b) The join: the GPE is the KE at the bottom — 4.8 J hands over. $KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, so $v^2 = 2 KE \div m = 2 \times 4.8 \div 1.6 = 6.0$.

$v = \sqrt{6.0} = 2.4$ m/s (2.45) — a sensible trolley speed. Write the $v^2$ line: in June 2025 (2H Q2(a)(ii)) it carried its own mark, and a wrong mass from (a) was carried forward through all three.

(c) The measured speed is lower because some of the energy is transferred to the surroundings by friction and air resistance (dissipated as heating), so less than 4.8 J is in the kinetic store. The mark is for where the energy went (friction / air resistance → the surroundings by heating); "lost" on its own names no destination.
(d) Stage 3, Topic 8: work done against gravity $= m g h = 52 \times 10 \times 3.0 = 1560$ J; power $= E \div t = 1560 \div 4.0 = 390$ W (2 s.f.).

questions.text: A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from a height of 1.8 m. $g = 10$ N/kg.

parts.text: Calculate the gravitational potential energy it loses as it falls.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate its speed just before it lands, assuming no air resistance.
parts.hint: The 9.0 J hands over to KE: $v^2 = 2\text{KE} \div m$.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The measured landing speed is 5.6 m/s. Explain the difference. (2)
parts.model:
• Some of the energy is transferred to the surroundings by air resistance (work done against it, dissipated by heating), so less than 9.0 J is in the kinetic store.
  • A smaller KE means a smaller speed — $v = \sqrt{2 KE / m}$ (the second mark is the destination — "lost" alone does not give it).
parts.label: c

questions.text: In a chain calculation, stage 1 gives a wrong energy. What should you do in stage 2?
options: Stop — no more marks are available
Use the wrong value, show the working, and label the stage: error carried forward lets stage 2 score
questions.explain: Mark schemes give a mark per stage.

questions.text: A heater of power 60 W runs for 5.0 minutes before its energy goes into $\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta$. The join needs…
options: $E = 60 \times 300 = 18\,000$ J, because t must be in seconds
questions.explain: Minutes to seconds at the join.

checklist: Name the quantity that each stage hands to the next before starting the arithmetic
Convert units at the join (kJ to J, cm to m, g to kg, minutes to seconds) before the next equation
Carry a stage's answer forward and label every stage, so error carried forward can score
sections.blurb: A long exam question rarely stays in one topic. It hands a quantity from one topic to the next — an energy, a force, a volume, a potential difference — and the marks sit at those hand-overs: the right equation picked for each stage, the units matched at the join, the number carried forward (even a wrong one), and each stage labelled so the examiner can give the stage its mark.

sections.title: One object, four stages: density, change of state, latent heat and specific heat capacity in the same question

parts.title: The chain
parts.html:
StageEquationHands overWatch
mass and density → volume$V = m \div \rho$ (Topic 14 / 15)$V$ in m³ or cm³keep the units the data use (kg and kg/m³, or g and g/cm³); do not round 0.0047 m³ to 0.005
solid vs liquid densityparticle spacing—the solid is usually denser: particles closer, more per unit volume; the same mass has a smaller volume
cooling curve → change of stateflat section = freezing at constant temperaturethe melting pointon a cooling curve the flat part is freezing, not melting; energy is transferred from the wax
mass → energies$Q = mL$ for the flat part; $\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta$ for the slopesenergies in Jsame mass in both, in kg (June 2024 2H Q3(c): 60.0 g into $Q = mL$ — $60 \times 2.26 \times 10^6$ scored 1 of 2); $L$ in J/kg (190 kJ/kg = 190 000 J/kg); $\Delta\theta$ is the temperature change

June 2025 2H Q5: all the wax liquid between which points (1), the particles' motion as it freezes (2), the volume of 3.9 kg of liquid wax at 830 kg/m³ (2), how the volume changes on solidifying at 930 kg/m³ (1), and why the solid's cooling R–S takes much less time than the flat freezing section Q–R, with $L = 190$ kJ/kg and $c = 2.1$ kJ/kg °C given (3). June 2024 2H Q3: the volume of 14.1 g of copper at 8.96 g/cm³ (3), why the solid is denser (2), the energy to vaporise 60.0 g of water with $L = 2.26 \times 10^{6}$ J/kg (2), and a volume read off a jug (2). Every stage is on the Topic 14 page; the exam asks them in one go.

parts.title: A block of wax
parts.question: 3.0 kg of liquid wax (density 800 kg/m³) is left to cool; the graph shows its temperature. Specific latent heat of fusion of wax = 180 000 J/kg; specific heat capacity of solid wax = 2100 J/kg °C. (a) Calculate the volume of the liquid wax. (b) State how the volume changes as the wax solidifies (solid density 920 kg/m³). (c) Calculate the energy transferred to the surroundings while the wax freezes. (d) Calculate the energy transferred as the solid cools from 70 °C to 40 °C, and use the two values to explain the shape of the graph. (9 marks)
steps: (a) $V = m \div \rho = 3.0 \div 800 = 3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ m³ (0.00375 m³ — keep the figures).
(b) The solid is denser, so the same 3.0 kg occupies a smaller volume ($3.0 \div 920 = 3.26 \times 10^{-3}$ m³): the particles pack closer in the solid.
(c) Join: the same 3.0 kg. Freezing at 70 °C (the flat section): $Q = mL = 3.0 \times 180\,000 = 540\,000$ J, transferred from the wax to the surroundings.
(d) Cooling the solid: $\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta = 3.0 \times 2100 \times 30 = 189\,000$ J.

The freezing section (6 min) is about three times as long as the cooling to 40 °C (2 min) because the specific heat capacity (2100 J/kg °C) is much less than the specific latent heat (180 000 J/kg) — the first 2025 mark, with both values quoted the second — so far more energy (540 kJ against 189 kJ, the same ratio) must leave the wax during the change of state than during 30 °C of cooling, and energy leaves at roughly the same rate throughout — so it takes longer.

graph.alt: Cooling curve for wax: 90 degrees at the start, falling to 70 degrees at 2 minutes, flat at 70 degrees until 8 minutes, then falling to 40 degrees at 10 minutes.

questions.text: A 250 g block of ice at 0 °C is heated until it is water at 20 °C. Density of ice = 920 kg/m³; $L = 334\,000$ J/kg; $c$ (water) $= 4200$ J/kg °C.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the ice.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to melt the ice.
parts.hint: $Q = m L$ with the same mass, in kg.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to warm the water to 20 °C.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Ice is less dense than water. Explain what this means for the volume of the water compared with the ice. (2)
parts.model:
• Density = mass ÷ volume and the mass is the same (conserved in the change of state).
  • A larger density (water, 1000 kg/m³) means the same mass has a smaller volume: the water occupies less space than the ice did ($0.250 \div 1000 = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ m³).
parts.label: d

questions.text: A copper wire has a mass of 22.4 g. Copper has a density of 8.96 g/cm³. Calculate the volume of the wire.
On a cooling curve the flat section is much longer than the sloping section before it. Explain why, using the words latent heat and specific heat capacity. (3)
questions.model:
• The flat section is the change of state (freezing), and the specific heat capacity is much less than the specific latent heat — quote both values (e.g. 2100 J/kg °C against 180 000 J/kg) — so the sloping section needs less energy than the flat one (June 2025 2H Q5(e): one mark for the comparison, one for the values).
  • Energy is transferred from the substance to the surroundings at about the same rate throughout…
  • …so transferring the larger amount of energy takes a longer time.

checklist: Carry one mass through $\rho = m/V$, $Q = mL$ and $\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta$ with the units matched
Explain the solid/liquid density difference and the cooling curve's flat section with the particle model
Compare the energies in a cooling curve using the latent heat and specific heat capacity values
sections.blurb: A lump of wax, a coil of copper, a block of aluminium: the question gives its mass once and then walks through density (a volume), a change of state (the particle picture and the cooling curve) and the thermal equations (latent heat, specific heat capacity). The join is the mass — the same number in every stage — and the trap is a unit that changes between stages (g/cm³ in one line, kg in the next).

sections.title: Pressure, force and particles: one pressure question across three topics
equations: P = \dfrac{F}{A} \ \rightarrow\ F = PA \text{ (normal to the surface)}

parts.title: The chain
parts.html:
StageEquation or ideaHands overWatch
force directionfluid pressure acts normal to the surface, towards it (Topic 15 / 9)an arrowfrom the point, at right angles
pressure and area → force$F = PA$ (Topic 15)$F$ in Narea in m²; a difference in pressure if fluid is on both sides; round as asked
graph → descriptionpressure decreases as height increases; non-linear; quote numbersa reading, a % change(new − old) ÷ old × 100
description → particlesless air above → smaller weight of air → lower pressure; the air is less dense: particles further apart (Topic 14)—do not say gravity is weaker higher up (ignored, 2023); the three credited reasons are less dense, less air above, lower temperature (2023, Nov 2021); density is about spacing, not particle size

June 2024 2H Q4: the direction of the water's force at X (1), the force from a skate on ice from $4.8 \times 10^{7}$ Pa and $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ m² to 2 s.f. (3), describe the pressure–height graph (2), read 8850 m (1), the % change from 104 to 74 kPa (2), and explain the density change with height using the particle model (2). June 2023 2H Q4 did the aeroplane window: pressure difference, $F = PA$, the larger window, the arrow, the graph and the reason.

parts.title: The skate and the mountain
parts.question: (a) An ice skater of weight 600 N stands on one blade with an area of $2.0 \times 10^{-5}$ m². Calculate the pressure on the ice. (b) Atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa at sea level and 70 kPa at 3000 m. Calculate the percentage decrease. (c) Explain, using the particle model, why the air at 3000 m is less dense than at sea level. (7 marks)
steps: (a) $P = F \div A = 600 \div (2.0 \times 10^{-5}) = 3.0 \times 10^{7}$ Pa — a huge pressure from a small area, which is why the blade bites into the ice.
(b) Change $= 70 - 101 = -31$ kPa; percentage $= -31 \div 101 \times 100 = -31$ % (a 31 % decrease; divide by the original value).
(c) At 3000 m there is less air above, so a smaller weight of air presses down on the air there…
…so it is less compressed: its particles are further apart — fewer particles in each cubic metre — which is a lower density (Topic 14: density depends on spacing).

questions.text: A submarine hatch has an area of 0.60 m². The water outside is at a total pressure of 400 kPa and the air inside the submarine is at 100 kPa.

parts.text: Calculate the net pressure on the hatch.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the net force on the hatch.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The force of the water on the hatch acts…
options: at right angles to the hatch, towards the inside
parts.explain: Normal to the surface, towards it.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Explain why the total pressure outside is greater at a greater depth. (2)
parts.model:
• Deeper down there is a taller column of water above the hatch, which has more weight.
  • That weight acts over the same area, so the pressure due to the water is greater (plus the same atmospheric pressure on the surface).
parts.label: d

questions.text: A graph shows atmospheric pressure falling from 100 kPa at sea level to 50 kPa at 5.5 km and 26 kPa at 10 km. Describe the relationship and explain it. (4)
questions.model:
• As height increases the pressure decreases.
  • The relationship is non-linear (the line is curved, not straight; doubling the height does not halve the pressure): quote two pairs of values — 100 kPa at 0 km, 50 kPa at 5.5 km, 26 kPa at 10 km — the fall per km gets smaller (2023: a mark for 'use of numerical data', at least two pairs).
  • Higher up there is less air above, so a smaller weight of air presses down.
  • The air higher up is also less dense — its particles are further apart because less air presses on it — so each extra kilometre of height removes less weight.

questions.text: A pressure of $1.5 \times 10^{5}$ Pa acts on a window of area 0.35 m². Calculate the force on the window, to 2 significant figures.

checklist: Turn a pressure into a force on a surface with $F = PA$, drawn normal to the surface
Describe a pressure–height graph with numbers and explain it with less air above and lower density
Explain the lower density with the particle model: particles further apart
sections.blurb: The 2023 and 2024 pressure questions each ran through three topics: an arrow for a force (Topic 9), a calculation with $P = F/A$ (Topic 15), a graph of pressure against height, and then 'explain with the particle model' (Topic 14). The joins are a pressure handed into $F = PA$ and a graph handed into an explanation.

sections.title: Springs with forces and energy: graph, spring constant, free-body diagram, resultant

parts.title: The chain
parts.html:
StageEquation or methodHands overWatch
graph → energyarea under the weight–extension line: $\tfrac{1}{2} F x$ (Topic 15)$E$ in J$x$ in metres (2025: cm left in, 100 times too large)
graph → spring constantgradient, or $k = F \div x$ from a point on the line$k$ in N/mgive the unit that matches the $x$ you used (June 2025 2H Q8(c)(ii): 45 N/m and 0.45 N/cm both scored 2; 45 or 0.45 with no unit scored 1)
block in equilibrium → free-body diagramweight down, tension (spring force) up, equal length, through the centre (Topic 9)a diagram2025: vectors "must have a size as well as a direction"; arrows near the edge of the box would make it spin
two forces at an angle → resultantscale drawing, tip to tail, measure the closing side (Topic 9) [H]$R$ in Nstate the scale; measure the length and convert

June 2025 2H Q8: why the vertical spring is longer than the horizontal one (its own weight stretches it) (1), what the extension equals — the loaded length minus the unloaded vertical length Y, not the horizontal length X (1), energy from 0 to 8 cm from the area (3), the spring constant with its unit (2), two vectors on the 5 N block (2), the resultant of 4 N and 5 N at X by scale drawing (2). June 2023 2H Q7: the pen spring's force, the change in length, the accuracy point, the hook's force (6 N up) and the resultant of 30 N and 40 N.

parts.title: The spring and the block
parts.question: The graph shows the weight hung on a spring against its extension. (a) Calculate the energy stored at an extension of 20 cm. (b) Calculate the spring constant and give its unit. (c) A 4.0 N block hangs at rest from the spring; describe the free-body diagram. (7 marks)
steps: (a) Area of the triangle to 20 cm: $E = \tfrac{1}{2} F x = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8.0 \times 0.20 = 0.80$ J (extension in metres).
(b) $k = F \div x = 8.0 \div 0.20 = 40$ N/m (or $E = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2$: $0.80 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times k \times 0.20^2$ gives the same).

(c) Two vectors through the centre of the block: weight 4.0 N downwards and the force of the spring 4.0 N upwards — both labelled 4.0 N and the same length, because the block is in equilibrium (resultant zero); in June 2025 (2H Q8(d)) the label on both arrows was the second mark.

graph.alt: Weight against extension for a spring: a straight line from the origin through 20 cm and 8 N.

questions.text: Use the weight–extension graph for the spring.

parts.text: Calculate the energy stored when the extension is 10 cm.
parts.hint: Area of the triangle to 10 cm (weight 4 N), x in metres.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the extension when a 6.0 N block hangs from the spring, in cm.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The 6.0 N block hangs at rest. Describe the two force vectors that a free-body diagram of the block must show. (2)
parts.model:
• The weight, 6.0 N, drawn vertically downwards from the centre of the block.
  • The force of the spring on the block (tension), 6.0 N upwards through the centre, labelled 6.0 N like the weight and the same length, because the block is in equilibrium.
parts.label: c

parts.text: The block is now pulled along a table by one string with 6.0 N and a second string at right angles with 8.0 N. Find the resultant of the two pulls (by scale drawing or otherwise).
walkthrough: tip to tail at right angles: $R = \sqrt{6.0^2 + 8.0^2} = 10$ N (a scale drawing gives the same)
parts.label: d

graph.alt: Weight against extension for a spring: a straight line from the origin through 20 cm and 8 N.

questions.text: A 2025 free-body diagram of a block on a spring scored one mark of two because…
options: the arrows were the wrong colour
the arrows were not labelled 5 N — the label on both arrows was the second mark
questions.explain: Two vectors, equal length, through the centre.

questions.text: A vertical spring is longer than an identical horizontal one with nothing hanging on either. Why?
options: The vertical spring is stretched by its own weight

checklist: Find the energy stored from the area under a weight–extension graph and the spring constant from its gradient
Draw the free-body diagram of a block hanging in equilibrium: two vectors, equal, through the centre
Carry the block's weight from the spring equation into the force diagram
sections.blurb: The 2023 and 2025 spring questions moved from Topic 15 into Topic 9 half-way through: the energy from the area under the graph and the spring constant, then a free-body diagram of the hanging block, then the resultant of two forces by scale drawing. The joins are an extension in metres and a weight that appears in both the spring equation and the force diagram.

sections.title: Upthrust into density into moments: two chains in one question

parts.title: The chains
parts.html:
StageEquationHands overWatch
two weights → upthrustupthrust $= W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{liquid}}$ (Topic 15)a force in Nthe loss in weight, not the reading in the liquid
upthrust → volumeupthrust = weight of liquid displaced; $V = \text{upthrust} \div (\rho_{\text{liquid}} g)$$V$ in m³the liquid's density, not the block's
weight in air → mass; mass and volume → density$m = W \div g$; $\rho = m \div V$ (Topic 14)$\rho$ in kg/m³sense check: metals 2000–20 000 kg/m³
the weight → a load on a levermoment $= F d$; sum of clockwise = sum of anticlockwise in equilibrium (Topic 9)an effort in Ndistances from the pivot, in the same unit

June 2025 2H Q9: why the newton-meter reading differs in liquid and air (2: upthrust, equal to the weight of liquid displaced, the liquid denser than air); the block's density from a liquid of $1.4 \times 10^{3}$ kg/m³ (4, one mark per stage, error carried forward); then the winch 6-marker (Topic 9 T7). June 2023 2H Q6: a push-up pivot, moments on an arm holding a ball (equilibrium shown, then the muscle force with 15 N added), and the same ball floating in fresh and sea water.

parts.title: A block, a liquid and a lever
parts.question: A metal block weighs 8.0 N in air and 6.0 N when fully submerged in a liquid of density 1250 kg/m³ ($g = 10$ N/kg). (a) Calculate the density of the block. (b) The block is then hung 0.10 m from the pivot of a lever; calculate the effort needed 0.40 m from the pivot on the other side to balance it. (6 marks)
steps: (a) Upthrust $= 8.0 - 6.0 = 2.0$ N = weight of liquid displaced; mass of liquid displaced $= 0.20$ kg; $V = 0.20 \div 1250 = 1.6 \times 10^{-4}$ m³ — the block's volume.
Mass of the block $= 8.0 \div 10 = 0.80$ kg; $\rho = m \div V = 0.80 \div (1.6 \times 10^{-4}) = 5000$ kg/m³.
(b) Join: the block's weight in air, 8.0 N, is the load. Moment of the load $= 8.0 \times 0.10 = 0.80$ N m.
In equilibrium the effort's moment equals it: effort $\times 0.40 = 0.80$, so effort $= 2.0$ N — a lever that quarters the force.

questions.text: A stone weighs 12.0 N in air and 9.0 N when fully under water (density 1000 kg/m³). $g = 10$ N/kg.

parts.text: State the upthrust on the stone.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the stone.
parts.hint: Weight of water displaced = 3.0 N → mass 0.30 kg → volume.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the density of the stone.
parts.label: c

parts.text: The stone is hung 0.25 m from the pivot of a uniform beam balanced at its centre. Calculate the force needed 0.75 m from the pivot on the other side to keep the beam level.
parts.hint: Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment with the stone's weight in air.
walkthrough: moment of the stone $= 12.0 \times 0.25 = 3.0$ N m
parts.label: d

questions.text: Explain why the newton-meter reading is smaller when the stone is in water than in air. (3)
questions.model:
• In the water there is an upthrust on the stone, so the stone has an apparent loss in weight (the meter reads weight − upthrust) — the 2025 scheme's first phrase.
  • The upthrust equals the weight of water displaced by the stone.
  • Water is much more dense than air, so the water displaced weighs far more than the air displaced did — the upthrust in air is negligible.

questions.text: In the worked example's chain a student uses the reading in the liquid (6.0 N) as the upthrust instead of the loss in weight (2.0 N). On the 2025 marking, this…
options: took one mark off and carried the error forward through the other three stages
questions.explain: Each stage is marked; errors carry forward.

questions.text: A ball floats in fresh water and then in sea water. Compare the upthrust on the ball in the two liquids, and explain why less of the ball is under the surface in the sea water. (3)
questions.model:
• The upthrust is the same in both: the ball floats, so in each liquid the upthrust equals the ball's weight (= the weight of liquid displaced).
  • Sea water is more dense than fresh water…
  • …so a smaller volume of sea water has the same weight as the ball: less needs to be displaced, so less of the ball is below the surface (June 2023 Q6(c)).

checklist: Run the four-stage chain from loss in weight to density, carrying each stage forward
Use the object's weight as the load in a moments calculation
Explain why the upthrust on a floating object is the same in two liquids and what changes
sections.blurb: The 2025 paper's last question was two chains back to back: a block weighed in air and in a liquid became a density (Topic 15 into 14), then a lifting machine became a 6-mark moments-and-gears explanation (Topic 9). The 2023 paper paired moments on an arm with a ball floating in two liquids. The joins are a volume, and a weight that reappears as the load.

sections.title: Work, efficiency, GPE and power: the lifting questions

parts.title: The chain
parts.html:
StageEquationHands overWatch
force and distance → work$W = F d$ (Topic 8): the load's weight × the height lifted = useful workan energy in Jdistance in the direction of the force
useful → totalefficiency $=$ useful ÷ total, so total $=$ useful ÷ efficiency (Topic 3)an energy in Jdivide by the efficiency, do not multiply; as a decimal
wastedtotal − useful—say where: friction in the pulley bearings, lifting the pulley's own moving parts, the rope stretching
energy → height, or → power$\Delta h = \Delta GPE \div (mg)$; $P = E \div t$$h$ in m, $P$ in Wmass in kg (320 g = 0.32 kg); time in s

June 2023 2H Q9: the barrel's weight from 1800 J of work over 1.2 m (2), the total work at 64 % efficiency (2), another reason for wasted energy (1), and the 6-mark plan "investigate how the efficiency of the pulley system varies with the weight being lifted" with a spring balance, metre rule, pulley and metal cubes — "include how you will use your measurements". June 2024 2H Q7: distance from $W = Fd$, an experiment to find the GPE gained by a lifted mass naming the measuring devices (4), the height from 5.8 J and 320 g, and one reason a motor is under 100 % efficient. June 2025 2H Q2(b): a student's power climbing stairs to 2 s.f.

parts.title: The pulley
parts.question: A pulley system lifts a crate 2.5 m. The useful work done on the crate is 4000 J. The system is 60 % efficient. (a) Calculate the weight of the crate. (b) Calculate the total work done by the person pulling the rope. (c) The person pulls 10 m of rope; calculate the force they pull with. (d) The lift takes 16 s; calculate the useful power. (7 marks)
steps: (b) Join: 4000 J is the useful energy. Total $=$ useful ÷ efficiency $= 4000 \div 0.60 = 6700$ J (6667; about 2700 J wasted against friction in the pulleys and lifting the lower pulley block).
(c) The person's work is the total: $6667 = F \times 10$, so $F = 670$ N — less than the crate's weight, over four times the distance.
(d) Useful power $= E \div t = 4000 \div 16 = 250$ W.

questions.text: An electric motor lifts a 0.450 kg mass through 1.6 m in 2.5 s. The motor transfers 9.0 J of electrical energy during the lift. $g = 10$ N/kg.

parts.text: Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by the mass.
parts.hint: $m g \Delta h$ with the mass in kg.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the motor as a percentage.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the useful power output of the motor.
parts.hint: $P = E \div t$ with the useful energy.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Give two reasons why the motor is less than 100 % efficient. (2)
parts.model:
• There is friction in the motor's bearings, so energy is transferred to the thermal store of the motor.
  • The current in the motor's wires has a heating effect (electrical heating), so energy is transferred to the surroundings as well as to the mass. (June 2024 2H Q7(d): friction (1), heating (1); sound is ignored.)
parts.label: d

questions.text: Devise an experiment to investigate how the efficiency of a pulley system depends on the weight being lifted. You have a spring balance, a metre rule, the pulley system and metal cubes. Include how you will use your measurements. (6)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row below, any 6 of the 7.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VariablesIndependent: the weight lifted (number of cubes); dependent: the efficiency; control: the same pulley, the same height lifted, pulling steadily.
2RelationshipEfficiency = useful work ÷ total work = (weight × height) ÷ (pulling force × rope pulled).
3ChangeLift one cube, then two, three … (weigh each load with the spring balance).
4MeasureHeight the load rises and length of rope pulled, with the metre rule; the pulling force, with the spring balance in the rope; the load's weight.
5UseCalculate useful work = weight × height and total work = force × rope length for each load; efficiency = useful ÷ total; plot efficiency against weight.
6AccuracyPull slowly and steadily (constant speed, so the balance reads the force); read the balance at eye level; measure heights from the same reference point.
7RepeatRepeat each load three times and take a mean efficiency.
  • Any six of the seven points; the 2023 question asked for how the measurements are used, so the Use row is essential.

questions.text: A student of mass 55 kg climbs a flight of stairs 4.2 m high in 6.0 s. Calculate her power, to 2 significant figures. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: Work $= m g h$; power = work ÷ time.
walkthrough: Units: W — write 385 W then 390 W: the 2 s.f. line is its own mark, given for rounding whatever you got (June 2025 2H Q2(b))

checklist: Find the useful work from a force and distance, then the total energy from the efficiency
Plan the pulley-efficiency investigation with the seven steps, including how the measurements are used
Find a height from a GPE and a power from an energy and a time, to the figures asked
sections.blurb: A pulley lifting a barrel, a motor lifting a mass, a student running upstairs: work done becomes useful energy, efficiency divides it by the total, and power divides it by time. Three joins — an energy, a fraction, a time — and a 6-mark plan to investigate efficiency that the seven steps answer.

sections.title: Electrical energy as a store: the electric car

parts.title: The chain
parts.html:
StageEquationHands overWatch
mass and speed → KE$KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ (Topic 3)$E$ in Ja car's KE is $10^5$ J; a battery stores $10^8$ J
battery energy and motor power → time$t = E \div P$ (Topic 8)$t$ in s → hours1 kWh $= 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J; convert before dividing
charging → energy$E = I V t$, or $P = IV$ then $E = Pt$ (Topic 10)$E$ in J, $t$ in s"comment on this claim" (June 2023 2H Q8(d)): calculate the time, then one sentence — the claim is / is not justified because the time is less / more than … (the conclusion mark is independent of the arithmetic)
current and time → charge$Q = I t$ (Topic 10)$Q$ in Chours into seconds first
regenerative brakingKE → electrical (the motor runs as a generator, Topic 13) → chemical store of the battery—instead of the thermal store of the brakes: less energy wasted, longer range

June 2023 2H Q8: the car's KE (2), how long the battery lasts (2), how regenerative braking extends the range (2), whether a charging-time claim is right using $t = E \div (IV)$ (3), and the charge moved (2). The evaluate mark is for the comparison and a conclusion, not just the number.

parts.title: The electric car
parts.question: An electric car of mass 1200 kg travels at 16 m/s. Its battery stores 36 kWh ($1.3 \times 10^{8}$ J) and its motor has an average power of 18 kW. The charger supplies 32 A at 230 V and the maker claims a full charge takes 'under 5 hours'. (a) Calculate the car's kinetic energy. (b) Calculate how long the battery can run the motor, in hours. (c) Comment on the charging claim. (d) Calculate the charge that flows during the charge. (9 marks)
steps: (a) $KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 16^2 = 153\,600$ J $= 150$ kJ — give it in the unit the question asks for (June 2023 2H Q8(a): 'in kJ'; 153 600 scored 1 of 2). About 0.1 % of the battery.

(c) Charging power $P = IV = 32 \times 230 = 7360$ W; $t = E \div P = 1.3 \times 10^{8} \div 7360 = 17\,700$ s $= 4.9$ hours — so the claim of under 5 hours is just right, but only if nothing is wasted in the charger and battery; in practice it would take a little longer.

questions.text: An electric scooter of mass 90 kg (with rider) travels at 8.0 m/s. Its battery stores $1.8 \times 10^{6}$ J and its motor's average power is 250 W. It is charged at 2.0 A from a 230 V supply.

parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the scooter and rider.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate how long the battery can run the motor, in minutes.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the time to recharge the battery fully, in hours.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Calculate the charge that flows during the recharge.
parts.hint: $Q = I t$ with t in seconds.
parts.label: d

questions.text: Explain how regenerative braking increases the distance an electric car can travel on one charge. (3)
questions.model:
• When the car brakes, its kinetic energy is transferred to the motor, which runs as a generator (induction)…
  • …so energy that would otherwise be wasted (heating the brakes) is transferred electrically to the chemical store of the battery (June 2023 2H Q8(c): kinetic store (1) → chemical store (1)).
  • The battery therefore has more energy after braking than it would with friction brakes, so the car can travel further before it needs charging.

questions.text: A charging calculation gives $t = 3.6 \times 10^4$ s. The claim says '8 hours'. The evaluation should say…
options: $3.6 \times 10^{4}$ s is 10 hours, so the claim is too optimistic — and real charging wastes some energy, making it longer still

checklist: Find a kinetic energy and compare it with a battery's energy to get a time
Use $E = IVt$ (or $P = IV$ and $E = Pt$) to check a charging-time claim
Find the charge moved with $Q = It$, in coulombs
sections.blurb: An electric car's question joins Topic 10 to Topic 3 through energy: the kinetic energy comes from the battery, the battery's energy divided by the motor's power gives a running time, and charging it back is $E = IVt$ with a charge $Q = It$. Watch the units at every join — kWh to J, hours to seconds.

sections.title: Induction with its neighbours: dynamo, transformer, diode, motor, grid, loudspeaker

parts.title: The chain
parts.html:
StageIdea or equationHands overWatch
turning → induced pdthe coil cuts field lines, a pd is induced; with a lamp connected a current flows and the induced current's field opposes the motion, so it is harder to turn (Topic 13) [H]a pd, then a current"induced", never "produced"
primary → secondaryalternating current → changing field in the core → changing field through the secondary → pd induced (Topic 13) [H]$V_s$d.c. would give no changing field
turns → pd; pd → current$V_p \div V_s = N_p \div N_s$ [H, P]; $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$$V_s$, $I_s$step-down: fewer turns on the secondary, larger current
a.c. → charging a batterya diode lets current flow one way only, so the battery is charged, not discharged on the reverse half-cycles (Topic 10)d.c.a battery needs d.c.
motor beside generatorthe commutator connects the coil to the battery through the brushes (carries the current to the coil); it reverses the current in the coil every half turn; so the force on the coil stays in the same direction and it keeps turning the same way (June 2025 2H Q6(d): one mark each) (Topic 12) [H, P]—the loudspeaker is the motor effect; the microphone is induction — the same parts, opposite direction of transfer (Topic 13 T4) [P]

June 2025 2H Q6: how a current is produced in the secondary (3), the secondary turns from 230 V, 1.5 V and 1840 turns (2), why a diode is needed in series with the battery (2), the commutator (3). June 2023 2H Q10: how the dynamo was turned between readings, why it gets harder to turn with a lamp (2), the secondary pd (3), loudspeaker versus microphone (6). June 2024 2H Q10: the falling magnet and its investigation, then the grid transformer 11 000 V → 230 V (6). The standard chains are on the Topic 13 page word for word; this is where they are asked side by side.

parts.title: The toothbrush charger
parts.question: An electric toothbrush is charged through a transformer with 1150 turns on its primary, connected to 230 V a.c.; its secondary gives 12 V. A diode connects the secondary to the rechargeable battery. (a) Explain how a pd is induced in the secondary coil. (b) Calculate the number of turns on the secondary. (c) Explain why the diode is needed. (d) The primary current is 0.050 A; calculate the secondary current, assuming no energy is wasted. (9 marks)
steps: (a) The alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core; the changing field passes through the secondary coil; a changing field through a coil induces a pd across it [H].
(b) $V_p \div V_s = N_p \div N_s$: $230 \div 12 = 1150 \div N_s$, so $N_s = 1150 \times 12 \div 230 = 60$ turns [H, P].

(c) The secondary pd is alternating, but a battery must be charged with current in one direction (d.c.); the diode conducts only one way, so it blocks the half-cycles that would drive current the wrong way through the battery.
(d) Join: the transformer's output. $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$: $230 \times 0.050 = 12 \times I_s$, so $I_s = 0.96$ A — stepping the pd down steps the current up.

questions.text: A bicycle dynamo is turned by the wheel and lights a lamp.

parts.text: Explain why a pd is induced in the dynamo. (3)
parts.model:
• The coil (or magnet) moves relative to the magnetic field, so the coil cuts magnetic field lines.
  • A pd is induced across the coil (the field through the coil is changing).
  • Because the coil is in a complete circuit with the lamp, the induced pd drives a current.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Explain why the wheel is harder to turn when the lamp is switched on. (2)
parts.model:
• With the lamp connected a current flows in the coil, and the current has its own magnetic field.
  • The current's magnetic field interacts with the magnet's field, giving a force that opposes the motion (a force against the turning), so more work must be done to keep the dynamo turning — the extra work is the energy transferred to the lamp. (Do not say the resistance is greater — ignored in 2023.)
parts.label: b

parts.text: The dynamo supplies the lamp with 6.0 V at 0.50 A. Calculate the power transferred to the lamp.
parts.label: c

questions.text: A step-down transformer in the grid takes 11 000 V and gives 230 V. It supplies a street with 150 A at 230 V.

parts.text: The primary has 9600 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the current in the primary, assuming the transformer is 100 % efficient.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Explain why electricity is transmitted at 11 000 V rather than at 230 V. (3)
parts.model:
• For the same power, a higher pd means a smaller current ($P = IV$).
  • The energy wasted by heating in the cables depends on the current ($P = I^2 R$), so a smaller current wastes much less energy.
  • Transformers step the pd up for transmission and down again to 230 V for homes, so the saving comes at no cost in usable energy.
parts.label: c

questions.text: A coil of wire attached to a cone sits in a magnetic field. Compare how it works as a loudspeaker with how it works as a microphone. (4)
questions.model:
• Loudspeaker: an alternating current in the coil produces a changing magnetic field around it → the two fields interact: a force on the coil that changes direction (motor effect) → the coil and cone move back and forth → the cone pushes the air: sound.
  • Microphone: sound makes the cone and coil move in the field → the coil cuts field lines → a pd is induced → an alternating current with the same frequency as the sound.
  • Both use the same parts — a coil, a magnet, a cone — and in both the frequency and amplitude of the current match the frequency and amplitude of the sound (both credited in the 2023 indicative content).
  • The direction of transfer is opposite: electrical → sound in the loudspeaker (motor effect), sound → electrical in the microphone (induction).

checklist: Explain the dynamo (harder to turn with a lamp) and the transformer (why a current flows in the secondary) in the standard chains
Use the turns-ratio and pd–current equations and carry the output into the circuit that follows
Compare the loudspeaker with the microphone, and explain the diode and the commutator in the same question
sections.blurb: The induction questions never stay in Topic 13: a dynamo's output goes to a lamp (Topic 10), the transformer's output through a diode to a battery, a motor's commutator sits next to the transformer, and the loudspeaker is compared with the microphone (Topic 12 beside 13). The join is a pd — induced in one place, used in the next.

sections.title: Electricity into heat: a heater's energy into a temperature rise

parts.title: The chain
parts.html:
StageEquationHands overWatch
current, pd, time → energy$E = IVt$, or $P = IV$ then $E = Pt$ (Topic 10)$E$ in J$t$ in seconds; a joulemeter reads $E$ directly
energy → temperature rise$\Delta\theta = \Delta Q \div (mc)$ (Topic 14)$\Delta\theta$ in °Cmass in kg; this assumes all the energy went into the substance
measured rise → c$c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$$c$ in J/kg °Ccomes out too high if energy went elsewhere
why smallerenergy transferred to the surroundings and to the container / heater parts—2024: ignore "energy is lost" and "not 100 % efficient"

June 2024 2H Q9: the temperature rise of a 5.8 kg storage-heater brick given 210 kJ with $c = 860$ J/kg °C (2 — the kJ must become J), why the actual rise is smaller (2), and the 6-mark SHC-of-water practical (Topic 14 T6: immersion heater, joulemeter or ammeter and voltmeter with a stopwatch, balance, thermometer; Level 3 needs $\Delta\theta$, the energy and how $c$ is found). The Topic 10 heating-effect explanation sits underneath: the current's electrons collide with the ions of the heater wire and transfer energy to them, so the ions vibrate more — a higher temperature (June 2018 2H Q8(c): one mark for each).

parts.title: The heater in the water
parts.question: A 12 V immersion heater draws 4.0 A for 5.0 minutes in 0.40 kg of water ($c = 4200$ J/kg °C). (a) Calculate the energy supplied. (b) Calculate the expected temperature rise. (c) The measured rise is 7.5 °C; calculate the value of c this gives and explain why it differs from 4200. (7 marks)
steps: (b) Join: 14 400 J into the water. $\Delta\theta = \Delta Q \div (mc) = 14\,400 \div (0.40 \times 4200) = 8.6$ °C (8.57).
(c) $c = \Delta Q \div (m\Delta\theta) = 14\,400 \div (0.40 \times 7.5) = 4800$ J/kg °C.

It is too high because some of the heater's energy was transferred to the surroundings and to the beaker, heater and thermometer, so the water received less than 14 400 J and its rise was smaller than expected; dividing the full energy by the smaller rise overestimates $c$.

questions.text: A 230 V kettle element carries 8.0 A and is switched on for 2.0 minutes with 0.80 kg of water in it ($c = 4200$ J/kg °C).

parts.text: Calculate the energy supplied by the element.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise of the water if all this energy goes into it.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The measured rise is 60 °C. Explain the difference. (2)
parts.model:
• Some of the energy is transferred to the surroundings (the air, by heating from the kettle's outside).
  • Some heats the kettle itself (the element, the body) rather than the water — so the water receives less than 220 800 J. (Name where it went, not "lost".)
parts.label: c

questions.text: A storage-heater brick of mass 6.0 kg ($c = 850$ J/kg °C) receives 255 kJ from its heating element overnight. Calculate its temperature rise.
Describe how to find the specific heat capacity of a metal block using an electric heater, a joulemeter, a balance, a thermometer and a stopwatch. (6)
questions.model:
6 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1MassMeasure the mass of the block with the balance.
2Set-upPut the immersion heater in one hole of the block and the thermometer in the other (a drop of oil for contact); lag the block.
3EnergyConnect the heater through the joulemeter; record the initial temperature; switch on and time the heating; read the energy supplied from the joulemeter (or $E = IVt$ with an ammeter and voltmeter).
4TemperatureRecord the final temperature; $\Delta\theta$ = final − initial.
5Calculate$c = \Delta Q \div (m \Delta\theta)$ — or plot temperature against energy and use the gradient.
6AccuracyLag the block to reduce energy transferred to the surroundings; wait for the highest reading after switching off; repeat.
  • Marked by levels: Level 3 needs the temperature change, the energy supplied and how $c$ is found from them.

checklist: Find the energy supplied by a heater from I, V and t (or P and t) with t in seconds
Hand that energy into $\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta$ to predict a temperature rise, or into $c = \Delta Q \div (m\Delta \theta)$
Explain why the measured rise is smaller, naming where the energy went
sections.blurb: The specific-heat-capacity practical is an electricity question for its first half: the energy supplied is current × pd × time, and only then does it become $mc\Delta\theta$. The 2024 storage-heater question handed 210 kJ from the heater into a brick; the 6-marker asked for the whole practical with electrical measurements. The join is the energy in joules, and the trap is minutes.

facts.q: What is 'the join' in a blended question?
facts.a: The quantity one stage hands to the next — an energy, a force, a volume, a pd. Name it before the arithmetic.
Find it; match units there; carry forward and label each stage; check the number makes sense.

facts.q: Stage 1 wrong — what about stages 2 and 3?
facts.a: Use the wrong value, show the working, label the stage: error carried forward still scores the method marks (and usually the answer).

facts.q: One object, four stages: the join?
facts.a: The mass — the same number in $V = m/\rho$, $Q = mL$ and $\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta$.
Freezing at constant temperature; $Q = mL$; energy from the substance to the surroundings.

$F = PA$, normal to the surface; use the pressure the question names — the difference only when it asks for the net (resultant) force (2023: the net force scored 1 of 2 when the question said 'due to the cabin air pressure').

facts.q: Less dense air higher up, in particles?
facts.a: Less air above presses on it, so the particles are further apart: fewer per m³.
Area $\tfrac{1}{2}Fx$ (x in m) and gradient $F \div x$ (N/m).

facts.q: Free-body diagram of a hanging block at rest?
facts.a: Weight down and spring force up, through the centre, both labelled with the value (equal lengths).

facts.q: The 2025 upthrust-to-density chain in one line?
facts.a: Loss in weight = upthrust = weight of liquid displaced → volume → mass from weight in air → density.

facts.q: The block's weight after the density stage?
facts.a: It becomes the load in the moments stage: moment = weight × distance from the pivot.

facts.q: Total energy from useful and efficiency?
facts.a: Total = useful ÷ efficiency (divide, as a decimal).
Useful = weight × height; total = pulling force × rope pulled; efficiency = useful ÷ total.
$W = mgh$, then $P = W \div t$, to the figures asked.
$3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J — convert before dividing by a power in W.
$t = E \div (IV)$; then compare with the claim and conclude.
KE → generator → electrical → battery's chemical store, instead of the brakes' thermal store.

facts.q: Why a diode after a transformer charging a battery?
facts.a: The secondary pd is a.c.; the diode passes current one way so the battery is charged, not discharged.
Same parts; loudspeaker is current → force → movement → sound (motor effect), microphone is sound → movement → induced pd → current (induction).
Fewer turns on the secondary, smaller pd, larger current ($V_pI_p = V_sI_s$).

facts.q: Heater energy into water: the join?
facts.a: $E = IVt$ (t in seconds) hands the energy to $\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta$.

facts.q: Why is the measured rise smaller?
facts.a: Energy transferred to the surroundings and to the container / heater parts — name where, not "lost".
The water got less than the heater's energy, so the rise was smaller; the full energy ÷ the smaller rise overestimates c.
